title: Decision Record: Annotation Types and the Sentinel

versions.body:
# Decision Record: Annotation Types and the Sentinel

Entity annotations and undefined values were initially covered in the same record for a simple reason: callers encounter both when specifying annotation arguments. The entity marker describes the object, while the default value needs to express "this argument was not provided." At the time, there was not enough information to determine how much of either object should be public, so the trade-offs were recorded first, without treating the notes as a complete interface.

There were two options at the time.

- Treat undefined values entirely as an internal processor convention. After reading the annotations, the processor maps unspecified arguments to an internal marker; the artifact needs no additional type.
- Keep an identifiable undefined state in the annotation artifact. The processor only consumes that state and does not independently define its meaning.

The first option keeps the public surface small. Annotation arguments can retain their usual syntax, and the processor can decide how to interpret them during generation. The problem is that external code needing to understand the arguments' meaning can only rely on the generator's implementation conventions. An ordinary object could be either a business value or a placeholder; the call site alone does not show whether it means "not specified."

The second option adds an interface to maintain, but separates the undefined state from ordinary arguments. This was the preferred direction at the time. That preference was not based on having validated every use case, but on the view that once entity annotations become a dependency, default semantics should not live only inside the processor.

Two questions also need to be kept separate here. The fact that the processor can read annotations only establishes a compile-time read path; it does not automatically mean runtime code can recognize the same annotation. The initial draft reached no conclusion about the runtime side, nor did it settle on a package name, type name, or creation mechanism.

Another unresolved point at the time was the size of the public surface. Even choosing to retain a sentinel entry point is no basis for treating helpers associated with the annotations as part of the interface as well. The initial draft's comparison was limited to "whether undefined should have its own identity"; it did not set default rules for each kind of argument, let alone list the generator's internal representations as referenceable objects.

The starting point for this review is recorded as `ktorm-ksp-annotations/ktorm-ksp-annotations.gradle.kts`. Start with that module to verify the declaration relationships in the annotation artifact, then decide the public boundary; do not infer that the interface is stable from a single successful generation run.

Decision: Do not adopt an arrangement where "all default semantics are interpreted solely within the processor." Keep public annotation types and a distinguishable undefined value as the preferred direction. The public surface, discovery method, and specific sentinel entry point still require follow-up review; if the runtime need does not hold up, the options should be compared again rather than treating this preference as an established fact.
versions.change_summary: Recorded the initial trade-offs for public annotations and the sentinel

# Annotation Types and Sentinels: Decision Record

This page originally recorded just one direction: entity annotations should not hide all decisions about defaults inside the generator. A later interface review changed how the question was framed. The question was no longer just "should there be an undefined value?" but at which layer annotation declarations, sentinels, and processors should each be stabilized. The concerns in the first draft still hold, so they have not been removed; but they do not answer how widely the types themselves should be visible.

## Old approach: start by leaving all semantics to code generation

There was an early verbal agreement: entity annotations would accept parameters, values left unspecified would be replaced with internal markers during generation, and external consumers would only need to care about the generated output. This could reduce the number of objects exposed by the artifact and avoid having to update an additional type alongside processor changes.

This approach is now marked **deprecated**. Not because a specific call has proved it necessarily wrong, but because it conflates two different questions: whether the annotation declaration is part of the artifact's interface, and how the processor interprets unspecified values. The former determines where references belong; the latter determines the generation flow. Leaving both on the generation side made it impossible to review either boundary independently.

There is also a historical reason to retain this text. At the time, there was not enough input to establish that runtime discovery was necessarily a required capability. Rewriting the old text in today's terms would make readers think validation involving reflection or the runtime environment had already been completed at the outset; it had not.

## Three options considered in the review

The review split the original either-or choice into three options.

**Option A: keep both annotations and default values on the generation side.**

This continues the early approach. Its advantage is the smallest public surface: the processor can fold different kinds of default parameters into its own internal representation. The drawback is equally direct: callers cannot see from the artifact what "unspecified" actually is, and multiple use sites can only maintain a shared understanding by following the same implementation conventions.

**Option B: expose annotations, keep undefined values internal.**

This option at least lets callers explicitly reference the entity marker. One view was that the generator would handle the undefined state, so there was no need to expose the sentinel through the interface as well. The objection was that making annotations public is not the same as making their default semantics public; if a parameter needs to represent undefined, visibility of the annotation type alone does not remove ambiguity at the call site.

**Option C: expose annotation types and retain an artifact-side entry point for the undefined state.**

This option separates "what type it is" from "how the generator handles it." The generator is no longer the sole authority on the meaning of undefined; instead, it consumes a state already expressed by the interface. The trade-off is that the public surface must be tightly constrained: temporary implementation names must not be treated as long-term commitments merely because they are close to the annotation module.

The disagreement among the three options is not about whether the processor still has a role. Under any option, the generation stage needs to read the annotations and process them. The real decision is whether consumers, before or outside generation, can use the types in the artifact to understand the entity marker and the unspecified state. Once this question was raised on its own, the review no longer treated "the processor already works" as sufficient justification for A.

This also changed the review order. First confirm whether the entity marker is a distinct type, then whether the undefined state is merely a convention for ordinary values, and only then discuss how the processor consumes them. The old order inferred the interface from a single generation result, making it easy to mistake incidental behavior from the internal implementation for an artifact commitment. The new order still does not automatically determine the final API; it only avoids bypassing the type boundary on the strength of successful generation.

This round did not make C the final rule. Checking back on `ktorm-ksp-annotations/ktorm-ksp-annotations.gradle.kts` can help locate the module, but it cannot identify all potential consumers, nor can the return relationships for every parameter be inferred from the build entry point. The review therefore made only a narrower decision: A is no longer the default path; B and C remain pending review of the actual public types.

## Correction to "discoverable"

The first draft conflated "the processor can read the annotation" with "the annotation is discoverable." The review separated them.

The processor reads annotations at compile time. This establishes that the generation step can obtain annotation information. Runtime discovery requires consumers to be able to obtain and identify the relevant types at runtime. The former cannot substitute for the latter, and one successful compilation cannot prove that the latter requirement has been met.

"Discovery" here also does not mean that "every caller must perform runtime checks." Some call sites only need stable type references; others need to identify the type at runtime. The review retained this distinction to avoid expanding the needs of one scenario into a shared workflow for all consumers.

At the time, someone suggested simply documenting that "the default means undefined," without introducing an additional type. This would reduce the interface surface, but would not resolve the type relationship: text can explain intent, but cannot give an ordinary object a distinguishable identity. If the same value could be interpreted as a valid value, a temporary placeholder, or a missing value, the call site would still have to guess.

The meaning of type safety here should also be kept narrow. It does not require all annotation parameters to share one defaulting mechanism, does not promise unlisted general-purpose conversions, and certainly does not turn arbitrary parameter values into sentinels. It is only a direction for the review: the undefined state should not be reduced to an unrelated generic object at the API boundary.

## Reservations in the review margins

An interim proposal once read:

> First have the processor fold unspecified parameters into the same internal object; if runtime identification is needed later, add a public type then.

The proposal retains its original meaning, but is now marked **no longer applicable**. The problem is not adding a type later in itself, but that deferring the public boundary lets callers develop their own interpretations of undocumented default values. By the time a type is added, it is already difficult to distinguish behavior that was merely coincidentally compatible from behavior that was intentionally promised.

Another proposal was to design a separate sentinel for each annotation parameter. It was not included in the scope of the decision. The available material only supports separating "undefined" from ordinary values; it does not establish that all parameters need the same level of default semantics. Expanding a local issue into a complete parameter system would exceed what this page could establish at the time.

As a result, this version's deferred items are more specific: the public location of the entity marker still needs to be checked; the conditions needed for runtime discovery still need confirmation; and whether the sentinel should be made available to callers through a creation or return entry point has not been decided. The three are related, but speculation about one cannot substitute for a conclusion about another.

## Decision in this version

The decision is to no longer accept an arrangement in which "the generator privately interprets all semantics." The annotation artifact should have a type boundary that can be reviewed independently; the undefined state should be distinct from ordinary parameter values; the processor is responsible for consuming these objects, not for redefining their interface semantics.

This version still does not fix package names, type names, or API names. Three categories still need to be checked: the public location of the entity marker, the conditions for runtime discovery, and whether the sentinel has a creation or return entry point available to callers. Subsequent review should start from the actual types, rather than working backward from generated results.

Three questions remain in the margins: what is the minimum set of public types; should the undefined sentinel appear as a constant or a creation entry point; and do callers that do not use runtime discovery still need a stable artifact boundary? These questions remain open.

# Annotation Types and Sentinel Decision Record

This record preserves several judgments from different stages. The earliest discussion concerned who should interpret the default value on an entity marker; the interface review then shifted the focus to the public boundary of the annotation artifact; only the latest follow-up review consolidated the relationship among the type, package, and sentinel into a verifiable decision. The old paragraphs were not cleaned up to match the current rules, because "generator-internal convention" was once a seriously considered option, and subsequent trade-offs must make clear why it was abandoned.

The module entry point is still recorded as `ktorm-ksp-annotations/ktorm-ksp-annotations.gradle.kts`. It corresponds to the build location of the annotation artifact and is also the first file opened when checking historical declarations. Here, we do not treat the build script as interface documentation: the script can help locate the module, but public types still need to be checked against the actual type boundary.

The module entry point and the public boundary were once conflated in the old records. The build location can show where the annotation artifact is assembled, but it cannot by itself answer whether a type should be referenced externally, nor can it show whether a neighboring implementation should be retained with the artifact over the long term. After they were separated, the follow-up work had a narrower sequence: first locate the annotation artifact through the module, then examine the relationship among the package, entity marker, and undefined state. This sequence did not elevate the build file into a design basis; it merely avoided skipping steps between the generated result and the interface object.

Likewise, the read path for KSP is only an input path. It indicates that the processor will encounter annotation declarations, but it does not mean that the processor has complete authority over the definition of annotation semantics. The two were initially placed side by side because the issue at the time came from the generation stage; the later interface review instead needed to consider separately the objects on the artifact side that could be referenced. The two passages discuss the same group of objects, but they do not answer the same question.

## Original Judgment from the Year 2023

The initial notes described the issue as "what should be given to the generator when no parameter is specified." This wording reflected the limitations of the time: it assumed that annotations primarily served the processor, and that as long as the declaration could be read during compilation, where the default semantics resided was merely an internal arrangement on the generation side.

The initial draft listed two directions.

- Have the processor replace an omitted value with an internal marker. The artifact provides only annotation parameters; the undefined state does not appear as an independent object.
- Give the undefined state a recognizable place in the interface, and have the processor continue generating after reading this state.

The first route had obvious appeal. The public surface was small, the processor could adjust its internal representation on its own, and no additional type had to be maintained for a default concept. There was also no complete list of consumers at the time, so it was impossible to establish that every referring party needed to know that the undefined value existed.

However, the initial draft still leaned toward the second option. The reason was not that the various usage patterns had already been verified, but that an ordinary value and "no value was provided" might look identical at the call site. If the undefined state were converted only inside the processor, external code facing an ordinary object would be unable to tell whether it was a valid value, a temporary placeholder, or a default marker. This ambiguity would not disappear merely because the generator could ultimately complete generation.

The initial draft did not settle on a type name, nor did it promise runtime detection. The only working judgment at the time was that the undefined state should not be reduced entirely to a processor-private detail; if it later turned out that the annotations truly served only at compile time, the public boundary should still be reconsidered.

### Omissions in the Original Record

The early text put "the processor can read annotations" and "annotations can be discovered externally" in the same sentence. This was a point that later needed explicit correction. Reading annotations through the processor is a compile-time path, proving that the generation step can obtain its input; runtime discovery concerns whether running code can obtain and recognize types. These are not the same capability, and a successful generation cannot replace checking the other side.

The semantics of all annotation parameters were not discussed at the time, either. The record covered only entity markers and the undefined state. Expanding it into a complete parameter design would attach a scope to the early material that was never present.

Another ambiguity left by the early text was that "distinguishable" was mistakenly phrased as though it meant some unified parameter encoding. The original intent here was narrower: callers should not have to infer solely from the processor implementation whether a value means unspecified. It did not require every annotation member to use the same sentinel, nor did it decide that default values would take the same form in every scenario. This limitation was retained later to avoid inventing an entire set of parameter rules just to fix one boundary.

## The Interface Split in Spring 2024

During the second revision, reviewers no longer treated "annotations" and "default values" as a single undifferentiated issue. The discussion separated the subject into three layers: the annotation declarations themselves, the values representing undefined, and the way the processor consumes the two. This separation made the original either-or choice insufficiently precise.

**Arrangement A: Keep both annotations and undefined values on the generation side.**

This continued the early proposal. The processor could fold together various kinds of unspecified parameters according to its own rules, while external consumers observed only the generated results. The advantage remained a minimal artifact surface. The disadvantage was that readers of the interface could not verify the identity of unspecified values on the artifact side; if different usage sites developed different interpretations, the issue could only be traced through the generator implementation.

**Arrangement B: Expose the annotations, while keeping undefined values internal.**

This arrangement resolved where entity markers could be referenced. Fang Ke is called to write and recognize annotation types, but when undefined parameters are involved, interpretation still depends on the generation side. Some reviewers considered this sufficient because the generator would ultimately process the parameters anyway; another view held that since annotations existed as an artifact interface, the boundary for expressing the undefined state should not be relegated entirely to implementation details.

**Arrangement C: Expose the annotation types and also retain an artifact-side entry point for the undefined state.**

This approach separates type identity from processor behavior. The generator consumes an already represented undefined state, rather than holding sole authority to interpret its semantics. The cost is that the public set must be carefully defined: helper implementations close to the annotation module should not automatically become long-term interfaces.

The reviewers did not treat A, B, and C as three labels to choose from based on preference. The cost of A was that consumers had only the generator implementation to trace; B preserved a place to reference entity markers, but did not answer what identity the unspecified state had in the interface; C required taking on the maintenance cost of additional types while separating referenceable objects from the processor's internal operations. This comparison weakened the explanatory power of the old claim that "the smaller the public surface, the better": a small surface was not the only goal, and whether the boundary could be checked independently also factored into the cost.

The meeting-page margin still contained a counter-question from that time: if runtime callers do not need to inspect annotations at all, can we return to A? The conclusion did not return to A. A stable reference location primarily serves the artifact boundary; runtime discovery is merely a usage pattern that requires an additional guarantee. Conversely, being recognizable to some runtime caller does not mean every adopter must use that path. This distinction prevents turning a possible usage into a fixed process for all callers.

The review did not immediately codify C as the final provision. A module path can help locate material near the declaration, but it cannot account for all potential consumers, nor can it imply that every parameter needs the same pattern. That decision was narrowed to just two points: Approach A is no longer the default route; subsequent reviews should focus on public types rather than continuing to infer the interface from generated output.

## Retained Transitional Approach

An earlier review draft contained the following suggestion:

> First have the processor fold all unfilled parameters into a single internal object; if runtime identification really becomes necessary later, add a public type then.

This suggestion is now marked **no longer applicable**, but remains in its original location. At the time, it was intended to avoid expanding the public surface too early, while acknowledging that the runtime side had not yet been confirmed. The problem is that once the public boundary is deferred, callers form their own interpretations around an unspecified default value. When the type is added later, it becomes difficult to distinguish which behaviors are merely accidentally compatible and which constitute intentional commitments.

During the same phase, there was also an idea to specify only in the documentation that a certain value represents undefined. It did not become part of the decision. Documentation can explain intent, but it cannot give an ordinary value an independent type relationship; consumers may still interpret the same value as a business value, an absence, or a placeholder. The only value of that idea was to remind us that reducing interface objects does not mean eliminating interface ambiguity.

Another unadopted expansion direction was to set an independent sentinel for each annotation parameter. The current issue does not require establishing a complete parameter system; it only requires making the undefined state distinguishable from ordinary values. There is no evidence that all parameters have the same level of default semantics, so a local boundary cannot be packaged as a system-wide design.

## Correction from a Follow-up Review

During a later follow-up review, the discussion at one point treated "compiles" as a sufficient criterion: as long as entity annotations did not obstruct generation, where the undefined value was placed did not matter. This criterion was later rejected. Successful compilation only shows that a particular generation path accepted the input; it cannot show what the artifact exposes to consumers, nor whether the undefined state is distinguishable at the type level.

This correction did not add any new generation commitments. The inspection target was merely changed from the generated result to public type relationships: whether the entity marker has a stable reference location, whether the annotation package constitutes an inspectable boundary, and whether the undefined state still retains an identity distinct from ordinary parameters. If only generated output is examined, all three may be obscured.

The review-page margin once contained the following exchange:

> Question: If a caller does not perform runtime checks, does the public type still have value?
>
> Answer: Yes. It first provides a stable reference location; runtime discovery is one scenario requiring a separate guarantee, not something that forces every caller to use the same approach.

This exchange does not replace the formal decision. It explains why the review did not revert to Approach A: some callers not currently using a particular capability does not mean the artifact can eliminate the type already needed to provide a stable boundary.

An imprecise formulation has also been corrected here: "discoverable at runtime" is no longer described as a natural consequence of the processor reading annotations. The former is a requirement that a type can be obtained and identified at runtime, while the latter is merely the fact that compile-time processing receives input. With the two separated, reviews can examine the entity marker and the generation path independently, without treating a pass on one side as validation of the other.

## The stopping point in 2025

Someone else took over KSP-201 on 2025-09-11 to continue the work, while the original owner switched to handling a production incident. The subsequent addendum did not approve closure: one point concerning the annotation types and the sentinel was still unconfirmed, and concrete input was missing, so it would not proceed to implementation. The next day, the card was marked as blocked because the upstream interface owner had not yet confirmed the input fields.

These records are not proof of the interface design, nor should they be presented as a finalized compatibility conclusion. They only explain why work stopped at the time. When the input fields are unconfirmed, no additional parameter semantics can be inferred from the card's status, and "someone is continuing to follow up" certainly must not be misrepresented as meaning that the public surface has already been finalized.

This stopping point also corrected a habit from the previous round: assuming that a public interface was already established simply because the module had annotation-related entry points. The entry points can be navigated to, but the type relationships still need to be checked individually. The earlier passages were not rewritten because the evidence available then differed from what was available later.

The card addendum's statement "do not proceed to implementation yet" applies only to the point where input was missing at the time, and does not revoke the earlier comparison of boundaries. It stopped implementation before field confirmation, but did not make the previously excluded internal private route the default approach again. Keeping this stopping point allows later readers to distinguish two kinds of unresolved issue: one where the interface scope still needs checking, and another where upstream input has not yet been provided.

## Several routes that have been ruled out

**Export only the generated output.**

This approach treats source annotations as pure input and considers generated tables or other artifacts to be what callers actually need. It does not fit the current problem because the objects under review themselves include the annotation types and the undefined sentinel. Describing only the generated output would erase the discoverability boundary for the original types.

**Represent undefined only in explanatory text.**

This approach provides no dedicated entry point and specifies only in prose that a certain value represents undefined. It cannot meet the requirements of the type relationships. Explanatory text can explain semantics, but cannot automatically give an ordinary value a distinguishable API identity.

**Include all adjacent types in the long-term public surface.**

This seems prudent, but would actually lock in implementation adjacency as well. The available material supports decisions only about the entity marker, the annotation package, and the undefined sentinel, and does not justify extending the commitment to auxiliary types that have not appeared. The public surface should stop at the objects that have been checked.

The exclusions above do not mean that only two objects remain in the annotation artifact. They only limit the objects this page makes decisions about: do not use "also in the same module" as a reason to expand the public commitment. If adjacent types that need to be referenced over the long term emerge later, their inclusion should be proposed based on their own interface relationships, rather than inferred as a corollary of the conclusion about the sentinel here.

## Current decision

After the above branching, stopping points, and corrections, it was decided to adopt an arrangement with explicit type boundaries on the artifact side. Annotation declarations are not merely private inputs to the processor; undefined state is not merely an internal convention; the generation pipeline consumes these objects but does not redefine their meaning.

The annotation artifact must expose a runtime-discoverable org.ktorm.ksp.annotation.Table, and org.ktorm.ksp.annotation.Undefined's `of` API must return a type-safe undefined sentinel.

The package boundary is org.ktorm.ksp.annotation. This decision covers only the annotation public surface in that package and the already-confirmed relationship between the entity marker and the undefined sentinel. It does not prescribe a uniform defaulting strategy for all possible annotation parameters, nor does it thereby imply any unlisted generated types, processing order, or adopter behavior.

This decision is more specific in scope than the previous version, but it does not inflate "public" into a generic term that any code can depend on at will. The entity marker has a type identity that can be referenced and checked; undefined state, through its API, preserves a relationship different from that of ordinary parameters; the processor consumes these objects during generation. All three must hold independently, which is why C is adopted here. Other objects within the module must still be evaluated according to actual interface needs and cannot gain equal status merely by sharing the same build location.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Annotation declaration
    Annotation declaration --> Runtime discovery
    Annotation declaration --> Undefined sentinel
    Undefined sentinel --> Generation pipeline
    Runtime discovery --> [*]
    Generation pipeline --> [*]
```

The two paths to the endpoints in the diagram are intentionally separate: runtime discovery concerns the annotation type itself; the generation pipeline concerns consuming the annotation and sentinel. They share the artifact boundary, but cannot substitute for each other. The fact that the processor once read a declaration is insufficient to prove that runtime code can discover it; likewise, a type being referenceable does not require every caller to use it through the generation pipeline.

The current verification focuses on the actual objects. First confirm that the annotation package exists as a public boundary, then confirm that the entity marker lies within that boundary, and finally confirm that, via its `of` API, the undefined sentinel returns a value that preserves the type semantics. The build module is the entry point for rechecking and should not serve as evidence in place of type checking; a single successful generation cannot replace checking the public relationship.

There are three interrelated reasons for choosing this route. The entity marker needs a type identity that is referenceable and checkable. Runtime discovery cannot be replaced by "the processor once read the declaration." Undefined state should maintain, at API, a type relationship different from that of ordinary values. Together, these rule out the earlier internal-marker route, but do not broaden the decision to encompass the entire annotation-parameter system.

## Adjacent issues not yet split out

Reference properties, naming strategy, and generated-table naming may likewise pass through the annotation artifact, but are outside the scope finalized by this decision. In particular, while the upstream input fields remain unconfirmed, we cannot incidentally prescribe how a reference property obtains its name from annotation parameters. That issue should remain in interface review, rather than being tacked onto the sentinel decision.

The compatibility representation to use during migration has also not yet been settled. If existing callers know only the conventions on the generation side, whether they need to explicitly switch to the public sentinel entry point depends on which adopters are in scope and the actual migration materials. No corresponding results are currently available, so the question is simply left open here, without speculating about the impact or setting unconfirmed completion criteria.

There is another easily overlooked boundary: the minimal set of public types is not the same as all types in the module. If the public surface needs to be expanded later, add a decision that identifies the specific objects; do not rewrite earlier text to make the history look as though the full scope was known from the outset.

## Appendix: Two Outdated Examples

### Old Example One: Representing the Default as an Empty Object

An early draft used "an empty object is sufficient to represent undefined" as an example. That example is now outdated because it sidesteps type distinctions: an empty object may be an ordinary value, or it may simply be a temporary placeholder at the call site. It is retained to explain why the sentinel was later required to have a clearly defined API, not to recommend continuing to use this representation.

### Old Example Two: Checking Only Whether the Processor Continues Generation

Another old explanation treated "the processor reported no errors and continued generation" as evidence that the type design was complete. That example is likewise no longer applicable. At most, it shows that the generation path accepted one input, not that entity annotations can be discovered at runtime or that the return relationship for undefined values has been established.

Neither old example should be used as a basis for new code or new reviews. They remain in the appendix to help readers understand why this page separates public types from generation behavior.

## Review Notes

The comments from the final review focused on one boundary: do not describe "public" as availability in a general sense, and do not describe "type safety" as an unconfirmed across-the-board guarantee. The current wording covers only entity markers, the annotation package, and the undefined sentinel. All other objects will continue to be handled through their respective interface reviews.

If subsequent materials call for changing the scope above, preserve this page's historical assessment and explain the newly added objects and the reasons in a new decision. The fact that the old proposal was overturned does not mean that the concerns at the time did not exist; it only means that the current public boundary no longer accepts an arrangement that leaves default semantics entirely to the generator.

# Enum References and SQL Annotation Proposal

Start by testing the enum reference and the SQL type in annotations separately; do not change both the generation logic and the annotation entry point in the first round.

The candidate approach for enum references is to retain the type description provided by the caller and resolve the actual enum type when processing the table field. Another option is to require the caller to provide a plain class first; it looks simpler, but would push parsing responsibility to every entry point, so it will not be adopted at this stage.

On the annotation side, first confirm in what form the SQL type should be exposed. The default-value syntax must be retained here; the annotation parameter must not be changed into an object that can only be supplied at runtime just to express type information.

This round prepares only minimal examples: one field reached through an enum reference and one annotation field with no explicit type configuration. A sample compiling does not mean the interface is finalized; we still need to see whether the code-generation side can obtain the same type information.

If the default value cannot be preserved, withdraw the annotation-side change first and continue checking enum references separately.

# Enum References and SQL Annotation Proposal

Last time, the two issues were tested in the same round; after review, they will still be handled through two separate entry points. Enum references concern whether the type description received by the processor can resolve to the target enum; the annotation SQL type concerns whether the public declaration can be expressed in the annotation without losing the type constraint. They converge during field generation, but they are not the same interface issue.

The code anchor examined this time is `ktorm-core/src/main/kotlin/org/ktorm/expression/SqlExpressions.kt`. The file shows imports of `BooleanSqlType`, `ColumnDeclaring`, and `SqlType`, showing that the expression side is already directly adjacent to the SQL type family. It is a suitable starting point for reviewing the type boundary, but does not replace checking the KSP annotation declaration itself.

Retain two options for the enum portion:

- The entry point accepts a type description, and the processor parses it before generating enum-related code;
- The entry point accepts only an already-resolved class.

The second reduces branching inside the processor, but makes the caller decide when to parse in advance. For enum fields in the reference chain, this prerequisite offers no clear benefit, so the first remains the trial direction. The point to confirm is that the resolved type is not generalized back into an ordinary object type during subsequent field generation.

On the annotation side, directly exposing a runtime SQL type instance is not recommended. Annotation parameters must be expressible in a declaration, and the default value must be retained; if the public signature erases the type upper bound for internal convenience, callers will later only be able to infer the actual type from generated output. The candidate is to let the annotation retain a type token, have the code-generation side read it, and map it to the SQL type.

The trial samples should cover these separately: an enum field entering the processor through a type description, an annotation using the default SQL type, and an annotation explicitly specifying a different type. The third item is not intended to expand the support scope; it is to prevent the default-value path and the explicit path from using two different declarations.

Do not target `SqlExpressions.kt` as the change point yet, and do not determine in this round whether existing callers need to migrate. If the enum sample succeeds only when the caller pre-resolves the class, withdraw the enum approach; if the annotation default value cannot be written into the declaration, withdraw the annotation approach and retain the existing entry point.

# Proposal for Enum References and SQL Annotations

This round narrows the interface work to two independent areas of change: input parsing for enum references, and how annotations express their public types. The earlier draft called both of these "field type issues," which made it easy to conclude that all type entry points should be replaced at once. After review, we will not take that approach. Enum references are handled as the processor obtains entity field information; the annotation's SQL type is the signature callers see when writing metadata. They share a generation pipeline, but rollback and compatibility checks should be separate.

On the expression side, `ktorm-core/src/main/kotlin/org/ktorm/expression/SqlExpressions.kt` remains the starting point for verification. The adjacency of `BooleanSqlType`, `ColumnDeclaring`, and `SqlType` there is enough to show that the SQL type is not just a single-string convention. Early notes used this to speculate that annotations should also directly expose internal SQL type objects; that speculation has been discarded. Annotation declarations need a type expression that can be written in source code, not a copy of the expression-side object representation.

## Enum References

Keep `TypeReference` as constructor input to `EnumSqlType`, rather than requiring every call site to supply a class up front. Resolving it in advance may look like a way to shorten the processor path, but it would actually scatter resolution timing across multiple entry points in the reference chain: some entry points have the entity declaration, while others only have a description of the field type. Enum-field failures would then become caller-specific failures, and the generation side would be unable to tell whether the class it receives came from the original reference.

This proposal only requires the processor to obtain the target enum type after receiving this input, then use that result in subsequent generation. It makes no new decisions about enum constants, ordinal storage, or JDBC mappings; these are outside the scope of this interface change. The earlier "class-only" alternative is retained here because it can still serve as a fallback: if a compilation entry point cannot provide a resolvable type description, keep that entry point on the old path to start with, rather than reducing type information for all entry points.

The interface requirement settled in this round is: EnumSqlType must accept TypeReference as constructor input and retain the resolved enum class as the type referenced by that TypeReference.

For validation, include an enum field reached through a reference and confirm that the class retained by the processor is the same enum that the input points to. Do not use only a directly specified enum class as the sample; that only proves the ordinary class branch exists, not that reference resolution has been retained. If this check fails, roll back the change to the enum construction entry point and continue using the existing working call path; do not roll back the annotation side with it.

## Annotation SQL Type

Annotation parameters cannot publicly return instances of the internal SQL type. Callers need to declare this value in source code, and switching to a generic interface must still allow existing default values to be written legally. During drafting, we considered reducing the type information to an unconstrained class. That would let the generation side keep working, but it would erase the `SqlType` constraint from the interface; we will not adopt it.

Use `KClass` to express the public type, retaining the generic upper bound of `SqlType`. This lets defaults and explicit types enter the processor through the same kind of annotation parameter; the generation side then reads the corresponding type token. This choice does not require enum references to go through annotation parameters as well; the two paths only share results when generating fields.

The current public contract is: the public return type of Column.sqlType must be expressed as KClass and retain the SqlType generic upper bound, while continuing to allow annotation defaults.

Before finalizing, keep at least two kinds of compilation samples: a field with no explicitly specified SQL type, and a field with an explicitly specified type. The former confirms that defaults can still be declared; the latter confirms that the upper bound has not been changed to an unconstrained class. For each sample, inspect the type read by the generation side, rather than only checking that the annotation source compiles.

## Migration and Rollback

This is not a proposal to migrate all field declarations. Whether existing callers depend directly on the return shape of `Column.sqlType` needs to be checked separately before release; this page does not contain that caller inventory. If existing declarations cannot be adapted to `KClass` and the generic upper bound while retaining defaults, roll back the public signature change first and retain the validation results for enum references.

Only after both the enum and annotation samples pass can this round's conclusions be handed off to the generation side for integration. One point still needs confirmation: whether existing annotation consumers have compile-time constructs that depend on the old return shape. The expression-side import relationships should not be used to answer that question.

# Java Module Descriptor Troubleshooting Tree

This record began with an investigation that initially attributed an error on the KSP side to the core query layer. The earliest starting point we can find is `ktorm-core/src/main/kotlin/org/ktorm/dsl/Query.kt`. The file is at `org.ktorm.dsl`, and its header shows imports related to `Database`, iterator, and expression. The text recorded at the time includes terms such as table, column, sqltype, type, java, ktorm, requires, and org, so it is not surprising that the search started in the query layer; but this starting point did not provide the module declaration itself.

At the time, we did not have the annotation artifact's declaration file, nor stable build output showing whether the error occurred before compilation, during compilation, or when consuming the artifact. The old record therefore preserves only the sequence of "where to start looking," without treating the path as confirmation of the cause. Java-related names appearing in a query file indicate, at most, that the file was within the search scope at the time.

Follow these branches first:

```text
Java-related error occurs
|
+- Can you find the descriptor file?
|  |
|  +- Yes
|  |  +- Read module, requires, exports
|  |
|  +- No
|     +- Record where it is missing and the build inputs
|     +- Do not infer module contents from the imports in Query.kt
|
+- Only Query.kt or old call names available?
   +- Keep them as navigation hints
   +- Do not start by changing dsl
```

The initial working hypothesis was that call relationships involving the query layer or table objects might connect the issue to a modularized path, so checking `Query.kt` first might narrow the scope. This hypothesis was not supported by excerpts from a module file or by even one reproducible failure. It was just a convenient place to start at the time.

The package in `Query.kt` only shows that the Kotlin file belongs to `org.ktorm.dsl`. Imports related to `Database`, iterator, and expression only show which objects the file interacts with directly. They do not show whether a package is exported by a Java module or whether a dependency is included in the module declaration.

If the query layer itself compiles, but the error still appears only with the annotation artifact or during modular use, stop expanding the search based on `Database` or expression names. The next step is to obtain the actual descriptor text; if the text is missing, just record the stage at which the error occurs and the available build inputs.

No fix steps are included here yet. Three things remain unconfirmed: what stable information is left when the descriptor is missing; whether the generated Kotlin types can help determine module boundaries; and whether the old link was merely the starting point for a past search. Once the actual declaration is available, add the results of checking the module name, dependencies, and exported packages.

# Java Module Descriptor Troubleshooting Tree

The first version left in the year 2023 started from `ktorm-core/src/main/kotlin/org/ktorm/dsl/Query.kt`. It was located in `org.ktorm.dsl`, and the file header showed imports related to `Database`, iterator, and expression. The issue text also contained terms such as table, column, type, and java, so checking the query layer first was not unusual. That version did not obtain a Java module descriptor; it merely listed it as a follow-up check.

The old entry points are still retained in the bookmarks. Some people entered through the issue name, while others entered through the call name; both entry points eventually landed near the query layer. They explain why the search historically started from core, not that the module descriptor is located in the query file, still less that the query file makes declarations about module contents.

### Original branch for 2023-06

```text
An issue occurs during modular compilation
|
+- Found Query.kt
|  |
|  +- First inspect call traces for table / column
|  +- Only imports are visible: return to build inputs
|  +- Kotlin compilation error: record it separately as a query-layer issue
|
+- Could not find Query.kt
   |
   +- Search for descriptor files
   +- Not found: note the artifact and the stage at which it occurred
```

The original working assumption was that the module issue might merely be a tail-end symptom of the generation process, and that handling the query layer or table code first might make the issue disappear. This assumption was not supported by experimental results. It can explain why the search started with familiar core files at the time, but it cannot serve as a recommendation for subsequent changes.

The initial version also contained an unverified inference: if table objects could be generated, the Java layer was probably already ready as well. This inference conflated the generated result and module consumption into a single stage. A generated type appearing in the result of one compilation only indicates that the generation process left a name behind; it does not indicate that the descriptor is available or that the consumer read the declaration.

### Margin note for 2023-06

One sentence was added during review: package, class names, and Java module descriptors are not the same kind of object. The `org.ktorm.dsl` in `Query.kt` is the location of the Kotlin file. `Database`, iterator, and expression are direct neighbors visible in the file header. module, requires, and exports belong to the descriptor text and must be read from the corresponding file or artifact contents.

This reminder did not immediately become a complete workflow because there was no stable way to obtain the descriptor at the time. It first solved a smaller problem: seeing a package name does not justify writing "visible in source" as "visible outside the module"; seeing a type imported does not justify writing "type adjacent" as "dependency already declared."

Therefore, when only `Query.kt` is at hand, the procedure is to preserve this path, record the stage where the issue occurred, collect the actual build inputs, and then stop to obtain the descriptor. Without a descriptor, do not fill in module relationships using package names, imports, or generated class names.

### Review of 2024-06

During review, three objects were recorded separately: ordinary Kotlin source files, generated Kotlin source files, and Java module descriptors. Ordinary source files are organized by package and imports; generated source files may carry table-class or annotation-type names; descriptors handle module, requires, and exports. Their appearing near one another in the same compilation does not mean that they can substitute for one another.

The direct dependencies of `Query.kt` can still serve as local reading clues. `Database` indicates that the query file is adjacent to database objects, iterator indicates that an iteration-related dependency is present in the file header, and expression indicates that the query implementation is adjacent to an expression object. The review obtained neither a module declaration from these names nor evidence that exported packages are determined by the query layer.

A reverse search was attempted at the time: list the objects visible in the file header, then trace Java module relationships from the names of `Database`, iterator, and expression. The result left no reliable descriptor excerpt, only the record "Not confirmed around Query." This attempt was later marked as failed, not because query API was unimportant, but because the search targets and the question to be answered were at different layers.

### Retained old judgments

The old page once said: "There is no problem around Query, so the module declaration can be ignored for now." This statement is no longer used. Normal query-layer compilation only means that no direct query-layer compilation problem has currently been observed; it does not mean that the module name is correct or that the dependencies and exported packages are correct.

Another old judgment was: "If a generated table class is visible, first assume that the annotation artifact can be consumed modularly." This is no longer used either. Generated classes and module declarations each need to be obtained separately. The former cannot testify for the latter, and the latter cannot explain every generation failure.

These sentences were not removed from the page because the old links still lead people here. Keeping them shows why the early investigation detoured to the query layer and lets later maintainers see which directions should not again be treated as confirmation steps.

### Revised stopping conditions

If the issue appears only during modular compilation, modular consumption, or annotation artifact loading, while the query layer has no reproducible Kotlin compilation problem, obtain the descriptor first. If the descriptor cannot be read, stop making judgments about module contents and retain the artifact, build inputs, and stage at which it occurred.

If the descriptor can be read, only then inspect module, requires, and exports separately. Do not substitute a package name for module, imports for requires, or class names in generated code for exports. If any item cannot be confirmed from the text, record only the missing item.

If the query layer also has an independent compilation error, retain it as a separate troubleshooting path. Do not modify DSL to pursue the module issue, and do not treat the module anomaly as gone just because the query-layer issue was fixed. Both paths can appear in the same build, but the existing record has not established a causal relationship between them.

### Distinction table for the year 2024

| Object observed | What it could establish at the time | Verification it cannot replace |
| --- | --- | --- |
| package of `Query.kt` | Package containing the Kotlin file | Java module name |
| imports of `Database`, iterator, and expression | Direct neighbors of the query file | requires and exports |
| Generated table class or annotation name | A name appeared in one generation result | Whether the descriptor can be read by the consumer |
| Descriptor file | Module boundary in the declaration text | Issues in other loading or build stages |

This table was added after the old misjudgment to separate search results from the scope of conclusions. It does not mean that all Java-related issues are module-descriptor issues. Ordinary Kotlin compilation, generation results, artifact layout, and consumption paths can all produce superficially similar phenomena.

### Still-unresolved areas

The second version still does not answer: whether the annotation artifact's declaration is consistent across different publication forms; whether dependencies take effect only on the modular path; whether artifact layout will still have an effect after packages are exported; or what identifiable output the build side will leave when the descriptor cannot be found.

The old links continue to point from the issue name or call name to `Query.kt`. They only explain where the historical investigation began and are insufficient to determine the module descriptor's contents. If the actual declaration is obtained later, add concrete text verification back to this page rather than continuing to treat query-layer imports as module evidence.
