# Java Module Descriptor Troubleshooting Tree

This page was not originally built around the module file. In month 6 of 2023, when the text from an investigation contained terms such as table, column, sqltype, type, java, ktorm, requires, and org together, investigators would usually open `ktorm-core/src/main/kotlin/org/ktorm/dsl/Query.kt` first. The file belongs to `org.ktorm.dsl`, and imports related to `Database`, iterator, and expression are visible at the top. For investigators at the time, this path was enough to explain why they had arrived at the core query layer, but it did not provide the Java module's declaration.

The old link was not removed. Some people treated it as the standard entry point for "look at Query first", while others continued from here to trace the use of table and column. This page retains that history and does not treat a familiar path as the place to modify the module. The later additions are kept in their original chronological order, and the old assessments are not rewritten to match the current answer.

The scope of this record has always been narrow: the Java module descriptor of the annotation artifact. Query DSL, table objects, generated source files, and consumer-side loading may all appear in the same investigation, but they belong to different layers. The early material put these layers into a single sequence of search steps, which is what made the issue look like an extension of Query.kt.

### 2023-06-21: The initial brief note

Initially, only a very short branch was recorded:

```text
A Java-related exception appears
|
+- Search for Query
|  |
|  +- Found table / column: continue with DSL
|  +- Only imports found: note the location
|
+- Generated code still provides no key information
   |
   +- Look for the descriptor file again
   +- Not found: stop at the build inputs
```

At the time, the module descriptor was treated as a fallback item at the end of the generation process, while the main cause was still thought more likely to lie in the query layer or table definitions. This assumption was not supported by excerpts from the module file or by consistent failure output. In the early notes, it served only to give investigators a starting point they could follow, and could not prove an implementation-level relationship between Query.kt and the module exception.

The earliest stopping conditions were also very limited: if only the query file and call names were available, record the missing build inputs; if the descriptor was available, then inspect module, requires, and exports. At the time, it had not been confirmed what text would be left if the module descriptor was missing, nor whether generated code could help determine module boundaries.

The initial draft implied an understandable but unverified idea: if table objects could be generated, the problem might already be far removed from the module layer. Only on later review did it become clear that this idea conflated "the generation process leaving behind types" with "modular consumers reading declarations". The initial draft contained no evidence linking the two, so this is retained as a working hypothesis from that time, not as a basis for action now.

### 2023-06-22: Review margin notes

After the review, a sentence was added in the margin: a package, a class name, and a Java module descriptor are not the same kind of object. The `org.ktorm.dsl` in `Query.kt` can only locate a Kotlin file; imports related to `Database`, iterator, and expression only show the direct neighbors visible in the file header. Even if a piece of source code can import a package, that does not imply that the package has already been exported as module API.

This reminder did not become a formal procedure at the time because there was not yet a stable entry point for obtaining descriptors. What it addressed first was confusion when reading: a source path can point to a file, but cannot substitute for a module name; imports can point to neighboring objects, but cannot substitute for dependency declarations; a generated class name can show that a name appeared in a particular result, but cannot substitute for the export scope.

The original "search for Query first, then look at Java" is still retained in the old example. It is useful for helping someone taking over for the first time find the historical context, but not for confirming module boundaries. At the time, if a search for Query led to `Database`, it should have been treated as a local code-reading clue, rather than continuing to infer the module's identity from the type name.

### The first round of misjudgments at the time

Early records once cited "no compilation errors in the query layer" as a reason to defer checking the descriptor. That sentence was later crossed out. The absence of direct compilation problems in the query layer only narrows the scope of the investigation on the query-layer side; it does not mean the descriptor is correct, nor does it mean the dependencies and exported packages are correct.

Another earlier judgment was that if the generated table classes could be referenced within the same compilation unit, the module configuration was probably fine. This judgment was not retained as a conclusion either. The presence of generated code only shows that the processing flow left behind types at some stage; non-modular compilation and modular consumption are not the same checkpoint, and the former cannot be used to vouch for the latter.

These earlier judgments are still kept here because old bookmarks land near this section. Deleting them would leave later readers seeing only the current procedure, without seeing why someone once started with the core query layer, or which steps have already been shown to be insufficient for confirming module contents.

### 2024-06-12: Reverse-search results

The second version tried listing the objects in the header of the `Query.kt` file, then working backward from names related to `Database`, iterator, and expression to identify Java module relationships. The search produced no actual module declarations, only a result of "unconfirmed around Query". This attempt was later marked as a failure, not because looking up API was unimportant, but because the search targets and the question to be answered were at different levels.

At the time, all that could be established was that three kinds of material were distinct from one another: regular Kotlin source files, generated Kotlin source files, and Java module descriptors. Regular source files are organized using package and imports; generated source files may contain table class or annotation type names; descriptors handle module, requires, and exports. They may appear in adjacent locations during the same compilation, but they do not carry the same evidentiary weight.

During the review, the information about `Query.kt` was condensed again into a limited-scope note: it is a query file in an existing Kotlin module, used for reading code and checking historical behavior. The `Database`, iterator, and expression in the file header show only direct adjacency. They do not provide the annotation artifact's module name, nor do they provide the dependencies it must read and the packages it exports.

From this round onward, when only `Query.kt` or an old call name was available, the procedure changed to preserving the path, recording the stage at which the issue occurred and the existing build inputs, then stopping to obtain the descriptor. Without a descriptor, package names, imports, or generated class names were no longer used to fill in module relationships.

### The old workflow in the margin is still there

The margin notes from 2024 once read: first search for `Query`, then search for `Database`, and finally check whether the generated code can reference table objects. This is suitable for gathering clues, but not for confirming Java module boundaries. This passage is retained because old bookmarks still lead people down this path, not so that those handling the issue later will follow it.

The same page also had the sentence: "If the generated code can reference the annotation package, the module setup is probably fine." This sentence did not distinguish between regular compilation and modular consumption, nor did it check the descriptor's dependencies or exports. A later note added: the generated output shows, at most, that the generation process reached a certain stage; it cannot replace the text of the module declaration.

If issues with generated types and issues with modular consumption appear at the same time in the same incident, first record the two symptoms separately. The former requires returning to the generation process and the resulting source files; the latter requires returning to the descriptor and the actual consumption path. Do not let one symptom serve as evidence for the other, and certainly do not group them under Query.kt just because both mention annotations or type names.

### The table of distinctions left from 2024

| Observed object | Scope it could establish at the time | Check it cannot replace |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The package of `Query.kt` | The package containing the Kotlin file | Java module name |
| Imports of `Database`, iterator, and expression | Direct adjacency to the query file | requires and exports |
| Name of a generated table class or annotation | A name appearing in one generation result | Whether the descriptor can be read by the consumer |
| Descriptor file | Module boundary in the declaration text | Issues in other loading or build stages |

This table was added after the earlier misdiagnosis to separate search results from the scope of the judgment. It does not mean that all Java-related exceptions belong to the module descriptor. Ordinary Kotlin compilation, generated source files, artifact contents, and consumer loading can all look similar on the surface; this page uses only the actual descriptor as the basis for module contents.

The last row in the table also has a boundary. Reading the descriptor does not mean that the exception has been resolved; it only means that verification of the declaration itself can begin. When all three types of text meet expectations but the exception remains, the subsequent issue may lie in actual compilation, artifact loading, or consumer loading. The current material does not specify a fixed order among these stages.

### The deprecated "fix the query layer first" approach

An operational recommendation was retained in an earlier draft: first handle the errors related to `Query`; if the table code can be generated, the Java layer would probably improve along with it. At the time, this provided an easy starting direction and fit the context that the query file was located in the familiar core path, but there was no corresponding evidence from a module declaration.

**This old approach is deprecated.** It is not valid to assume that module dependencies are determined by database objects just because `Database` appears at the top of the file; nor is it valid to infer exports from type names just because expression-related types can be referenced. The query layer may still have its own compilation or invocation issues, but that is a separate troubleshooting target.

If a module anomaly has no descriptor text, the stopping point should remain "module declaration not obtained", rather than changing DSL to produce a result that merely appears to show progress. Changing the query layer may alter other symptoms, but it will not automatically turn module, requires, and exports that were not originally read into confirmed text.

Another side effect left by the old approach is that troubleshooting records tend to say only "Query has already been checked". This does not specify what was checked, nor does it allow later people to determine whether the module boundary has already been read. If starting from the old entry point is still necessary, at minimum distinguish between: only opening the query file and obtaining the actual descriptor; only seeing generated types and reading the declaration text.

### Meeting addendum before 2025-08

Later, while organizing old records, someone pointed out that the phrase "Java-related exceptions" was itself too broad. It could refer to type issues during Kotlin compilation, boundary issues when annotation artifacts are consumed as modules, or simply finding the term java through an old link. Not all cases can be placed on the same branch just because their keywords overlap.

The meeting addendum did not provide new build commands or a standardized artifact layout. It only confirmed the handling sequence: first identify the stage at which the exception occurs; if it is already clear that the Java module boundary of the annotation artifact is involved, then obtain the descriptor text; if all that is still available is Query.kt and old call names, stop at historical navigation and do not modify DSL.

This sequence preserves the purpose of the earlier entry point. `Query.kt` can still help identify where searches started at the time, especially when old issue descriptions grouped table, column, type, and java together. But it no longer serves to verify module declarations.

### 2025-08-26: Consolidated troubleshooting tree

By the third version, some people were still coming in through the old Query entry point, so a more complete tree was retained. It applies only to scenarios where annotation artifacts are already suspected of involving Java module boundaries:

```text
A modularity-related exception involving an annotation artifact occurs
|
+- Is the actual descriptor text available?
|  |
|  +- No
|  |  |
|  |  +- Only Query.kt or a call name is available
|  |  |  -> Mark as old navigation, do not modify dsl
|  |  |
|  |  +- Build artifacts are available but no declaration text
|  |     -> Obtain the text; until then, stop assessing module contents
|  |
|  +- Yes
|     |
|     +- Does the module declaration belong to the annotation artifact?
|     |  +- No: stop at declaration identity
|     |  +- Yes: proceed to requires
|     |
|     +- Does requires already list the required dependencies?
|     |  +- No: stop at the dependency declaration
|     |  +- Yes: proceed to exports
|     |
|     +- Does exports include the packages needed for consumption?
|        +- No: stop at the export declaration
|        +- Yes: return to the actual compilation or consumption path
```

"Return to the actual compilation or consumption path" in the tree does not mean the exception has been resolved. It only means that the three types of text in the descriptor have been read. If the stage at which the exception occurs is still unclear, first specify whether it occurs before compilation, during compilation, after compilation, or during loading by the consumer; do not infer the stage from the package name.

The first branch of the tree specifically addresses the old entry point. When only `Query.kt` is available, do not treat `org.ktorm.dsl` as the Java module identity of the annotation artifact; when only `Database`, iterator, and expression are available, do not treat them as dependency declarations; when only generated type names are available, do not treat them as a list of exported packages either.

The second branch of the tree addresses cases where an artifact already exists but its text has not been obtained. The existence of an artifact can indicate that a particular build stage has run, but it cannot establish that the descriptor is included in it, has been read, or has been accepted by the consumer. Continuing to modify the query DSL at this point will not help; first obtain the corresponding declaration, then determine whether there is a problem with the module contents.

The last three branches of the tree only perform item-by-item verification. If any of module, requires, or exports does not match, record the specific missing item and the stage at which the issue occurs, then stop at the descriptor-handling stage. Do not skip the intermediate items and wrap up with "the package names look similar".

### Current descriptor verification

The current verification must target the annotation artifact's actual Java module descriptor, not `Query.kt`. First confirm that the file really belongs to that artifact, then read the module declaration, requires, and exports. Kotlin packages with similar names, generated classes, and old links can only help locate it; they cannot replace the text.

The Java module descriptor must be named ktorm.ksp.annotations, explicitly declare requires jdk.unsupported, and declare exports org.ktorm.ksp.annotation.

This guidance addresses only the descriptor itself. During verification, check the module name, dependencies, and exported packages separately; if any item is missing, record the missing item and the stage at which the issue occurs, and stop at the descriptor-handling stage rather than working around the problem by modifying `Query.kt`. If all three are present but the issue persists, do not claim that the descriptor is the sole cause either; take the verified text back to the actual compilation, artifact loading, or consumption path.

"Actual" has a specific meaning here: not module relationships inferred from the query file's imports, not external visibility inferred from the names of generated table classes, and not the location pointed to by an old bookmark. You can assess module, requires, and exports only after reading the declaration text corresponding to the artifact.

The current guidance does not require adding a call relationship at the query layer. The existing material only indicates that Query.kt served as a historical navigation point and that it is adjacent to `Database`, iterator, and expression; there is no implementation evidence connecting these objects to the annotation artifact's descriptor. Continuing to extend this chain would repackage the old mistaken conclusion as a more detailed mistaken conclusion.

### If issues still occur after the check

If all three items in the descriptor text have been verified, but the consumer still cannot access the expected type, first mark the descriptor check as complete, and do not go back to Query.kt to search for the same name. The next record should retain the stage at which the exception occurred and the actual build or loading materials, with follow-up handled through the corresponding path.

If the exception occurs during generation, verifying the descriptor cannot replace checking the generation process itself. If the exception occurs during loading on the consumer side, having generated source files cannot replace checking the loading path either. Both situations can occur alongside module descriptors, but the material on this page does not establish which comes first and causes the other.

If all that is known is "a Java-related exception" and no stage is given, do not directly apply the current descriptor conclusion either. First fill in the most basic information about the case: whether the actual descriptor has been obtained; whether each of the three items is present; where the exception occurs; whether the only entry point is an old link to Query.kt. If any of these is missing, this page stops at the layer already observed.

### Boundaries with adjacent naming records

The naming strategy, Reference Attribute Compatibility Naming and refs Collection Views also involve annotations, generated code, package names or type names. They are adjacent to this page in the KSP compatibility work, but answer different questions: the naming strategy handles the names of generated objects, refs handles views of referenced objects, and this page only verifies Java module declarations.

If a single case reports both incorrect generated names and a failure in modular consumption, first describe the two symptoms separately. Correct package exports cannot stand in for the naming strategy when assessing reference property names; correct generated class names do not justify skipping module declarations either. Older records put these topics under the same to-do item, only because they were adjacent in time, which is not a basis for merging their troubleshooting paths.

Name changes in adjacent records should not be fed back into this page either. This page does not infer the module name from table classes, refs objects or property names; likewise, it does not infer that these generated names must be correct from whether the descriptor is correct. When naming needs to be investigated, go to the corresponding naming record, rather than expanding the scope on the module page.

### Adjacent issues not yet split out

When all three descriptor items have been verified, but the consumer still cannot access the expected type, the available material provides no fixed order for choosing the first item to check among generated source roots, artifact contents and loading paths. For now this page retains only four fields for the case: whether the actual descriptor has been obtained; whether each of the three items is present; the stage at which the exception occurs; whether the only entry point is an old link to `Query.kt`.

This question cannot be answered with a blanket judgment. Different build entry points may expose failures at different stages, and generated output and loading issues may also appear at the same time. Once the person handling the case has the descriptor text, do not return to Query.kt to repeat the search; but until the stage of occurrence is known, do not attribute a cause to adjacent build or loading issues either.

If a new case can provide only a single old path, first record that the path is indeed still referenced, then add whether the actual descriptor can be obtained. Do not record "the link exists" as "the module declaration exists". If a new case can provide only a single generated type name, likewise first record that it is part of the generated output, and do not record it as a confirmed export scope.

### Outdated appendix: Quick confirmation method

**This appendix is retained for old links and is outdated.**

An early quick-check method was to open `Query.kt`, confirm that it could see `Database`, and then search for java among expression-related types; if there were many results, the provisional assumption was that there were no problems with the module configuration. This method did not read module, requires, or exports and can no longer be used as a verification step.

It was left in place because `Query.kt` is under the familiar core path, and query and table objects also readily give troubleshooters the feeling that they are "already close to the answer." When following old links, use it only to identify the historical context. The appendix's statement that "if there is no descriptor, there is no need to check modules" has also been retired: not finding a descriptor only indicates that the materials are incomplete, not that module boundaries do not exist.

Another outdated step was to modify the query layer first, then see whether the exception disappeared. It might change the surface-level error during a particular incident, but it did not read the declaration text or explain whether the original exception involved a module boundary. Now, when encountering the same entry point, first obtain the actual declaration or the corresponding text in the artifact, and refrain from making judgments about the module contents until that text has been obtained.

The old appendix was not removed so that old bookmarks would still have a destination. It is no longer an actionable verification procedure. Users arriving here should go to the troubleshooting tree above and first determine whether what they have is old navigation, generated output, or an actual descriptor.

### End-of-page notes

The issue that remains unresolved at the end of this page is not the lack of a longer call chain between Query.kt and the module descriptor, but which actual stage to continue from along the adjacent consumption path after the descriptor has been checked. The old entry points, failed attempts, review reminders, and outdated appendix are all retained here to help explain how past judgments were formed.

The current check goes only as far as the text of the actual Java module descriptor; beyond this boundary, move to the corresponding compilation or loading records, bringing along the stage at which the issue occurred and the materials already available.

# Base Table Generation Decision Record

This record did not originally start from a generator file. The old index placed "Base Table Code Generation" and `ktorm-core/src/main/kotlin/org/ktorm/entity/EntitySequence.kt` on the same search route, and later readers followed that route to trace back as well. The path is under the `org.ktorm.entity` package, and the direct dependencies visible at the top of the file are:

```kotlin
import org.ktorm.database.Database
import org.ktorm.database.DialectFeatureNotSupportedException
import org.ktorm.dsl.*
```

The local search also returned `table`, `column`, `entity`, `name`. These terms are enough to explain why the old entry point seemed credible: they relate to tables, columns, entities, and names respectively, and the same file also touches the database, dialect exceptions, and DSL. Early records therefore described this as "the entry point for base table issues". That wording was useful at the time, but it never provided a generator declaration, a processor entry point, or an output directory.

## The Two Options in the Initial Draft

The first approach was to treat `EntitySequence.kt` as the generation hub. The advantage was straightforward: the existing investigation could continue along `table`, `column`, `entity`, and `name`, keeping the threads connected without readers having to switch entry points. The problem was just as straightforward: if that premise did not hold, the subsequent explanations of base table objects, generation timing, and callers would all go off track with it. The file belongs to the entity package, but the excerpts currently retained show only entity-side declarations and imports; treating the package name and literal term matches as evidence of responsibility for generation would mistake runtime adjacency for compile-time output.

The second approach was to designate it as an entity-side entry point for tracing back. At the time, the presence of `Database` was not interpreted as "generation must go through a database instance", nor was the DSL import interpreted as "the file is a compile-time input". The old draft put these terms together in one explanation, making it easy for readers to mistake lexical proximity for a call relationship; this version keeps the options and their reasons separate.

Another direction considered was to rewrite the old entry point directly, replacing it with an "explanation of base table generation". It was not adopted. stateDiagram-v2

KSP-207 can serve as a navigation target on this page only after 2025-09-29. On 2025-10-01 it recorded `baseline_recorded`, and on 2025-10-08 it then moved from To Do to In Progress. They are sufficient to support the file's identity and the old search route, but cannot on their own support a decision that "base table generation is completed here". This distinction later became the most important revision to retain on this page.

## What Remains Undecided

"Base Table Code Generation" covered too much in the early records. Base table classes, entity access, table name resolution, and generated artifacts were once grouped into the same set of issue terms, but the current material has not broken them down into verifiable relationships. This page therefore does not fill in a new chain for them, nor does it interpret each of the four terms `table`, `column`, `entity`, `name` as a fixed stage. ## Outcome of This Decision

Continue to retain `ktorm-core/src/main/kotlin/org/ktorm/entity/EntitySequence.kt` as the starting point for tracing back to the old requirements; describe it as runtime adjacency on the entity side, not the base table generation hub. KSP-207 provides clues for later requirements, while `Users` serves only as a search identifier. This page does not fill in the generation entry point, call relationships, or artifact naming.

# Migration Notes for Generated Keys and URL Parsing

This record preserves the guidance used during a compilation-unit split. The handoff of generated keys from producer to consumer, and the parsing differences after the consumer encountered JDK URL text, were included in the same check to avoid another environment switch; the old draft did not treat them as two independent paths. When the record was revisited later, the original order was still not replaced in full. Clarifications were added only at a few points that were easy to misread.

The initial assessment was straightforward: if generated results were visible within the same compilation unit, assume the producer was working; after moving the consumer out, move it back to the original unit whenever compilation stopped. This treated the existence of the generated directory, the consumer seeing a type with the same name, and the consumer continuing to use already-visible symbols as a single outcome. The old draft did not retain the output for each case either; it simply attributed the failures to the split.

```text
Original check
Same compilation unit
      |
Producer generates keys
      |
Consumer continues compiling

Old approach after the split
Producer ──> Generated directory ──> Consumer
   |                                   |
   +------ Compilation stops ----------+
                    |
      Return to the original compilation unit
```

The migration sequence actually used at the time was as follows. First, keep the producer in its original compilation location; do not change the consumer in the same step. Once generated artifacts appear, move the consumer to another compilation unit. Continue recording subsequent observations only once the consumer can see the results in the generated directory. If this step stalls, the recovery action is not to continue switching the URL branch, but to stop the cross-module reference experiment, put the consumer back in the original compilation unit, and then remove the changes to the generated directory left by this round. This restores the old checking environment; it does not mean visibility after the split has been proven.

The old document placed URL at the end of this flow: only after the consumer failed would the parsing result for JDK be checked, with `URISyntaxException` used to search for exception text. This arrangement stayed in place because the aim at the time was to limit the scope of changes in a single integration debugging session. It also led to an overly broad attribution: whenever the URL branch appeared, the investigation would jump first to the core rowset-reading code, as though URL, generated keys, and JDBC value reads shared the same failure entry point.

The file listed at the time as the first place to look was `ktorm-core/src/main/kotlin/org/ktorm/database/CachedRowSet.kt`. The declaration directly visible there was `public open class CachedRowSet(rs: ResultSet) : ResultSet`. Nearby in the same file were `size()`, `getLocalDate(columnIndex: Int)`, `getLocalTime(columnIndex: Int)`, `getLocalDateTime(columnIndex: Int)`, `getInstant(columnIndex: Int)`, and `readTypeMap()`. The file was located at `org.ktorm.database`, and its header also showed imports of `InputStream`, `Reader`, and `BigDecimal`. On this basis, the old record treated date/time reads and URL parsing as compatibility work at the same location, and placed that work before cross-module referencing.

This part was later rechecked only at the file level; no new migration steps were produced. The rowset class retained its wrapper around `ResultSet` and these read entry points, but the old draft did not provide a direct connection between them and generated-key visibility. The original sequence was therefore kept on record as the old guidance: first look at rowset reads, then check cross-module generated keys. It had been used to organize the investigation and should not be read as a verified causal relationship.

When the old path needs to be restored during the split, follow the sequence in the original record: first stop the consumer's cross-module experiment; then put the consumer back in the producer's compilation unit; finally remove this round's changes to the generated directory. Do not treat exception text from the URL branch as evidence of a producer-side failure during recovery. The old draft presented the rollback as a case where the problem had been traced to generated keys, but that conclusion did not distinguish between the generated directory, consumer compilation, and parsing exceptions.

One gap remains: the exact input used for JDK URL parsing, and its relationship to the consumer-side path, were not included in this record. If this migration sequence continues to be used, the starting point should be the output actually left by the consumer; the date/time read entry points in `CachedRowSet` should not be used again to infer the URL branch.

# Extension Service Loading Decision Record

This record originally had only one not-entirely-reliable reading entry point. The old investigation traced the problem name and invocation name "Extension Service Loading" into `ktorm-jackson/src/main/kotlin/org/ktorm/jackson/EntityDeserializers.kt`. The entry point is still worth retaining: it was a starting point that actually appeared in the historical record, and it also explains why several later documents placed the Jackson side and the compilation-integration topic near each other. What needs to be corrected is not the entry point, but the step of jumping from the entry point to implementation ownership.

The scope that can be confirmed from the file header has not expanded. This is in package `org.ktorm.jackson`, and the directly visible dependencies are `JsonIgnore`, `JsonProperty`, and `JsonProperty.Access`. They are sufficient to show that this old lead is near entity handling and the use of Jackson annotations; they do not identify the object that declares the extension, the service discovery action, or the call site after assembly is complete. The early text did not spell out these distinctions, so on later reading it was easy to misread "was once investigated from here" as "the mechanism is here."

This time we still retain the draft's judgment: the path is a reading entry point, not an identification of the service-loading implementation. This judgment is slower than directly giving a seemingly complete module attribution, but it preserves room for materials added later. If the problem name is directly tied to the Jackson file, any reader seeing the annotation import may naturally assume that annotation processing participates in extension discovery; the existing record does not support this causal relationship.

## Keep the Starting Point, Narrow the Conclusion

The draft chose to retain the old path not because it had already proved anything, but because deleting the path would prevent later readers from seeing where the misreading came from. The historical investigation did not come out of nowhere: the problem name, invocation name, and this Kotlin file appeared in the same line of inquiry. Removing the file from the record would seemingly avoid misleading people, but in practice it would make the next occurrence of the same clue repeat a path that has already been taken.

On the other hand, retaining the entry point does not mean it can be written as a vague "related location." The term "related" is too broad and would make people stop distinguishing among the entity deserialization neighborhood, the extension declaration site, the service assembly site, and the call site. Here we use more specific wording: this file is retained only as the reading entry point for the old investigation; the package name and imports in the file header serve only as visible adjacent context; beyond that, no conclusion about the service-loading mechanism is currently drawn from this path.

This narrowing also applies to the three Jackson names in the file. `JsonIgnore`, `JsonProperty`, and `JsonProperty.Access` are neither extension configuration items nor service discovery markers here. They only describe the direct dependency surface of the old entry point. If a call snippet, extension declaration, or assembly material later clearly connects one of these objects to service loading, that relationship should be recorded near the material that shows the connection point, rather than looking back and interpreting the current import as evidence that the mechanism was already present.

Some had favored using "service" as a broad category label, counting any file involving pluggable processing as part of the topic. That approach was not adopted. It would collapse Jackson's entity annotation processing, Maven Extension Public API, generator actions, and service discovery into a single term, leaving readers unable to tell which layer a change affects. The topic needs to remain searchable, but its meaning must not be broadened to create a sense of completeness.

## What this decision addresses

"Extension Service Loading" remains a working topic on this page, not a confirmed class name, interface name, configuration key, or module name. This definition has a direct consequence: finding the term `ServiceLoader` does not justify asserting that it is central to the current chain, nor does a file's lack of that term justify excluding it from the reading scope. Service discovery may sometimes reside at the wiring point, and declarations and usage may also be scattered across different locations; the material provided so far has not identified any of these locations.

To avoid treating the topic as an implementation name, this page accepts only three types of partial evidence to advance its conclusions. The first can identify which object declares an extension. The second can explain how the declared object is discovered, registered, or wired up. The third can explain at which call site the wired object is actually used. These three types of evidence may come from the same location, or they may be separate. No single piece of evidence is required to answer all the questions at once.

This breakdown is not a new architectural design, but the minimum set of boundaries needed to document the assessment. If a piece of evidence provides only an extension declaration, it can narrow the first gap, but cannot answer the questions in the second and third gaps. If a piece of evidence provides only a call site, it can show where usage occurs, but does not necessarily explain which discovery mechanism the called object comes from. The easiest mistake to make during an early investigation is precisely to expand any partial observation into an end-to-end account from declaration to invocation.

The current Jackson path does not fit any of the three categories above. It provides a different historical fact: the earlier investigation once passed through the area around entity deserialization. This fact is not of low value, but its value is different. It can help readers revisit the source of earlier claims, but it cannot justify readers stopping their search for the actual locations of declarations, wiring, and invocations.

## Documentation approaches compared at the time

The first approach was to designate `EntityDeserializers.kt` as the implementation location. Its advantage is that the document is short and people searching by the issue name can quickly obtain a file path. The drawback is equally clear: the file header shows dependencies on Jackson annotations, not extension service declarations or wiring relationships. Presenting the path as the implementation location would cause later readers to mistake "start investigating here" for "this is responsible for loading". Once new evidence turns up elsewhere, this explanation ceases to be navigation and becomes a misattribution.

The second approach was to remove the old path entirely, leaving only a topic marked "yet to be confirmed". This option was also rejected. An item awaiting confirmation without an entry point would become detached from its historical context, leaving subsequent team members to restart their search from a very broad topic term, unable to tell at which step the earlier assessment had made a leap. Deletion would also erase the fact of its proximity to Jackson, as though it had never come up.

The third approach is to classify the topic directly as a KSP generation problem. The cards later did indeed contain `TestForUsers` and `generateTypes` as two search identifiers, so this hypothesis appears somewhat compelling. But the identifiers appear in a to-do item for finding conflicting material; that does not mean they are implementation names for service discovery, nor that the unconfirmed item occurred inside the processor. Classifying the topic as KSP generation based solely on search terms would replace missing call relationships with later navigation terms.

The fourth approach is to fold the topic into Maven Extension Public API and the generated-directory wiring. Both the Maven side and this page come up while reading through build integration, and after merging them it seems possible to obtain a longer "extension chain." But the public API, generated-directory wiring, and service discovery are not the same kind of fact. There is currently no material connecting the Maven lifecycle, generated directory, and compiler-plugin parameters to the Jackson entry point or service assembly. Merging them would only hide the gaps in different questions under a single name.

Therefore, the decision is: retain the entry point, retain the topic, and reject replacing the missing relation in the middle with either endpoint. This conclusion does not require future additions to resolve all the problems at once; it requires each addition to state clearly which segment it is filling in. In this way, new evidence can gradually reduce the gaps without turning the old entry into an implementation conclusion that, in retrospect, appears to have been clear all along.

## Reading Scope for the Old Entry

When starting to read from `ktorm-jackson/src/main/kotlin/org/ktorm/jackson/EntityDeserializers.kt`, first confirm whether what you are looking at is still the entity-processing area referred to by the old investigation. The package name `org.ktorm.jackson` and the three direct imports are the only currently visible anchors for this entry. Readers can use these to confirm that they have not jumped to a module with the same name but no relation; they cannot use them to infer that the deserializer is responsible for discovering extensions or that some Jackson annotation determines the order in which extensions are assembled.

The appearance of `JsonIgnore` only shows that this file directly uses this Jackson annotation. It does not show that the ignored property has a relationship to extension objects. The appearance of `JsonProperty` likewise only shows that the property annotation lies on this file's dependency surface; without a citable call snippet, property mapping cannot be treated as loading configuration. `JsonProperty.Access` is also merely the visible direct dependency type of `JsonProperty`; it should not be expanded into an access policy for some service.

These restrictions are not intended to exclude the file from the topic. On the contrary, they keep this entry usable: if it is later found that entity processing and extension assembly do indeed intersect, the intersection can be described precisely in terms of which symbol, call, or declaration it falls on, rather than vaguely saying, "The Jackson side is also related." The current material provides no intersection, so this page does not fill it in.

In the earlier investigation, the issue name and the call name pointed to this path. This wording must also be preserved literally. "Pointed to" describes only the movement of investigative leads, not the direction of code calls. The issue name may lead someone to the file, and the call name may appear while reading nearby material; neither is sufficient to prove that service discovery exists within the file. Recasting navigation verbs as dependency verbs was another leap that needed to be avoided earlier.

## New leads from KSP-216

After the initial draft was completed, KSP-216 became the task entry point for this topic. The to-do item on the card does not ask for direct confirmation of a particular service implementation, but rather for identifying two current sources with conflicting accounts of "Extension Service Loading" and confirming the maintenance page and the person responsible for updates. The card also provided two search identifiers: `TestForUsers` and `generateTypes`.

These two identifiers should be understood according to their use on the card. They help locate material that may be related to the topic, but cannot be recast on this page as service objects, discovery entry points, or a call sequence. `TestForUsers` may lead the reader to a generated artifact or related documentation, and `generateTypes` may lead the reader to a generation action or related documentation; the existing card text does not establish a relationship between them, nor does it say that either is responsible for extension loading.

The card's actual value is that it expands the question from a single code entry point into a check of "whether the current sources give consistent accounts". Previously, when only one old path was available, it was easy to assume that the task was simply to find the implementation file. KSP-216 shows that there was also a need at the time to confirm the maintenance location and responsibility for updates. This does not automatically mean that the conflict is a documentation naming issue, a difference in generated results, or an implementation difference; the card does not list the two sources or provide the conflicting sentences.

Therefore, this page does not reduce "two sources give conflicting accounts" to "just different wording". If the conflict comes from different sources' descriptions of the assembly location, the issue may involve implementation relationships; if the conflict comes only from titles or the maintenance page, the scope of the issue would be narrower. Without the source texts, the most accurate record is to retain the to-do item itself and its search identifiers, rather than fill in a passage describing the conflict on the card's behalf.

The initial draft did not cite KSP-216. The card appeared after the initial draft, so the new version uses it only as a navigation entry point for follow-up verification, without retroactively claiming that `TestForUsers` or `generateTypes` were already known when the earlier decisions were made. This time gap also shows that the initial draft's judgment to "leave ownership undecided for now" was not inferred from the card's text, but resulted from the code entry points visible at the time being insufficient to support a conclusion.

## Record card actions and technical decisions separately

KSP-216 Later, a support linkage appeared once. This action shows that the task was placed in a support context requiring continued handling, but it did not bring any new declaration, wiring, or invocation snippets. It can explain why the task is still being followed up, but it cannot be treated as implementation evidence for service loading.

Subsequently, there was one assignment change, with the stated reason that the joint-debugging work had moved to a new teammate and the card had been handed over as well. This reason only describes the movement of the on-site work. It does not say that the person taking over is responsible for the extension implementation, nor that any technical judgment has received sign-off from the implementation side. The joint-debugging handoff, module ownership, and release decision must be considered separately; the card handoff cannot be used to combine them into a single conclusion.

Afterward, a public update recommended checking the "current entry point and result" and explicitly noted that Extension Service Loading still had one unconfirmed item, with another update to follow when the next fact arrived. Here, its incomplete status is retained: the update calls for continued checking; it does not confirm that the two materials have been found, nor does it confirm that the service-discovery mechanism has been located. It further supports this page's decision not to close the gap prematurely.

The sequence of these three actions also cannot be used to prove the technical chain in reverse. Support linkage, task handoff, and continued checking are all records of work progress; they did not change the visible import at the old entry point, nor did they connect the search identifier to a specific extension object. Writing card actions as implementation decisions would allow nontechnical task workflow to replace confirmation of module relationships.

Regarding document responsibilities, this page retains the topic history, the misreading of the entry point, and the current decision; KSP-216 retains the task line for locating conflicting materials and the maintenance location. If clear declaration, wiring, or invocation material is found later, the technical record for the corresponding module should carry that relationship, with a limited explanation added to this page as needed. The quality side can use the existing materials to decide whether to let the work proceed through the gate, but a quality judgment does not replace confirmation of ownership of the module implementation.

## Maven-Side Material Is Not Used to Fill the Gap

DOC-22 covers Maven Extension Public API and Maven Generated Directory Wiring. It likewise falls within the scope of compilation integration and may also appear alongside this page when searching for "extensions". The link retained between the two records is for cross-reference lookup; it does not mean that the Maven extension and this topic are already part of the same implementation chain.

Combining the two pages was once considered an option. After they were combined, readers would get a seemingly continuous description: the Maven extension, the compiler plugin, the generated directory, and service loading would all be placed under "extensions". The cost would be that objects of different kinds would lose their boundaries. Maven's public API discusses interface exposure; the wiring of the generated directory concerns the placement of generated output; service loading, in contrast, requires actual declaration, discovery, wiring, or invocation material. Similar names cannot replace the connection between them.

The decision is to keep separate records. DOC-22 will continue to cover Maven interface and generated-directory issues; this page only records the legacy Jackson entry point, search leads for KSP-216, and the parts of the service-loading topic that have not yet been pinned down. If future material explicitly shows that a particular Maven interface, generated-directory setting, or compiler argument is involved in extension assembly, document that specific connection point, then add a scoped note between the two records.

This means this page does not describe the Maven lifecycle as the service-loading sequence, nor does it describe the generated directory as the location for extension discovery. The available material neither brings the Maven lifecycle into `EntityDeserializers.kt` nor connects the two search identifiers KSP-216 to Maven wiring. Linking these concepts prematurely would only turn a decision about a historical entry point into an unverified description of the toolchain.

## Current record status

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> HistoricEntry
    state "Reading entry point for the previous investigation" as HistoricEntry
    state "Topic pending verification" as Pending
    state "Retain entry point, leave association undetermined" as Decision
    state "Awaiting material on declarations, assembly, or calls" as EvidenceNeeded
    HistoricEntry --> Pending: The path is insufficient to explain the mechanism
    Pending --> Decision: Do not substitute issue names for code relationships
    Decision --> EvidenceNeeded: Continue adding material on specific parts
```

The states in the diagram are the processing states of this record, not runtime states of the code. The entry point for the previous investigation remains, the topic still needs verification, and the current decision limits the conclusions that can be drawn from the entry point; the next step requires material that can pinpoint a declaration site, assembly site, or call site. The diagram does not depict Jackson files, KSP-216, or DOC-22 as call nodes, because the available material does not provide call edges between them.

The current decision is as follows.

1. "Extension Service Loading" continues to be retained as a separate topic and is not equivalent to Jackson entity deserialization or to Maven Extension Public API.
2. `ktorm-jackson/src/main/kotlin/org/ktorm/jackson/EntityDeserializers.kt` is retained as a starting point for reading older troubleshooting material. Its `org.ktorm.jackson` package name and Jackson import statements are locally visible facts and cannot, on their own, establish the loading mechanism, implementation ownership, or call order.
3. KSP-216 is the task entry point for checking the current materials. The `TestForUsers` and `generateTypes` in the card are retained only as search identifiers until material explicitly connects them to declarations, wiring, or invocation.
4. Support links, integration-testing task handoffs, and updates on continued checks only indicate that the task is still being handled; they do not constitute sign-off on the extension implementation or establish module ownership.
5. Maven's public exposure of API and the generated-directory wiring remain within the scope of DOC-22. This page does not borrow Maven-side terminology to fill gaps in service loading.

Beyond the fifth point, the most important addition this time concerns how new material is recorded. When new material is added to this page, first identify whether it actually addresses declaration, discovery or wiring, or invocation and use. If the material is only a search result, a file path, or a one-sentence maintenance note, its original scope should still be preserved. It must not be elevated to a description of the complete mechanism just because it uses words such as "extension", "generation" or "service".

## Parts Still to Be Located

There is currently no material explaining what declares the extension objects. Nor is there material explaining how the objects are discovered, registered, or wired after declaration. The actual invocation sites have not been shown either. These are three distinct gaps in the implementation relationships; they should not be collapsed into a vague "service loading remains to be confirmed". When a code snippet becomes available later, first determine which gap it narrows, to avoid once again misrepresenting a single local detail as the complete answer.

The two pieces of current material mentioned in KSP-216 are also not listed on this page at present, so it is impossible to determine exactly where they conflict. The conflict may involve the maintenance page, the description of the generation chain, or the classification of the old entry point; the existing text does not contain enough detail to distinguish among these possibilities. The card's statement that "one more point remains unconfirmed" is likewise not identified as an issue of wording, generated output, or implementation differences. This page preserves these unresolved items and does not invent classifications on behalf of the task thread.

If the next piece of material is merely another code path, first record the objects directly observable from it and that path's relationship to the old Jackson entry point: a peer relationship, an upstream/downstream relationship, or a relationship that has not yet been established. If what is obtained is generated output, first determine whether it only provides clues about naming or artifacts, or whether it can point to actual calls. If what is obtained is maintenance notes, preserve the scope of the notes themselves, and do not expand a maintenance-oriented statement into an implementation mechanism.

Only when the same material, or materials that can be connected to one another, provides both the extension objects and the wiring calls is it appropriate to move the topic from "history and verification" to a more specific technical decision. Even at that point, the old Jackson entry point should remain in the history section, explaining where the earlier reading began, rather than being retroactively recast as a confirmed implementation location.

The current conclusion goes no further than this: the historical entry point can still be investigated, but the topic is no longer falsely attributed based on that entry point; KSP-216 continue to be used for checking the current materials; the Maven side remains independent. What is missing is not a smoother story, but material that can be tied to declaration, wiring, or call sites.

# Maven Extension and Directory Wiring Plan

This review first separates the Maven extension's public API from generated-directory wiring. Both go through the build process, but their acceptance criteria differ: the former checks what callers can obtain, while the latter checks whether the generated directory is actually included in the KSP compilation.

## Candidate Integration Approaches

The Maven extension could calculate and pass the generated directory directly, keeping the changes centralized, but lifecycle differences would then enter the extension. Alternatively, the KSP side could provide the directory information, with Maven only reading it and wiring it into the compilation phase. This makes the responsibilities clearer, but requires tighter version coordination between the two sides. The third option is to retain the existing build conventions and add a thin adapter on the Maven side. Rollback would be simple, but the risk of duplicate configuration would be relatively high.

Try the second option for now. Validate the public API first using the compiler plugin identifier and plugin options; evaluate directory wiring separately by looking at the discovery entry point, relative paths, and failure states, and do not treat internal helper functions as an interface contract.

`buildSrc/src/main/kotlin/ktorm.tuples-codegen.gradle.kts` can serve as an entry point for checking build declarations and adjacency relationships. # Maven Extension and Directory Wiring Proposal

When closing out KSP-COMPAT-2026.09, two Maven-side tracks must be validated separately: the public results the extension exposes to callers, and whether generated directories can feed into KSP compilation through the Maven lifecycle. v1 only listed the wiring approaches without spelling out the trial inputs or rollback conditions; this version narrows the scope based on outcomes and does not yet combine the Gradle convention plugin and Maven adapter into a single configuration.

## Test the Public API First

The regression item for KSP-217 requires observing results from the caller's side, not asserting on internal helper function names. The proposed public surface keeps `getCompilerPluginId` and `getPluginOptions`: the former should return the compiler plugin identifier, and the latter should build the options passed to the compiler plugin. The regression example only needs to verify caller-side access to these two methods on the Maven extension; whether both are implemented by the same class is left open.

Copying all defaults into Maven is not recommended here. The extension can assemble values already known to the Maven lifecycle, while compiler-related default behavior remains handled by the existing KSP interface. This avoids having two sets of default rules evolve independently during upgrades. The trade-off is that the version boundary between older extensions and KSP must be confirmed separately. If older Maven projects must rely on the full set of defaults within the extension, create a separate compatibility plan rather than expanding the public API as an incidental part of this trial.

## Directory Wiring Trial

KSP-222 left an entry point for post-upgrade regression testing of generated-directory wiring. Start at `buildSrc/src/main/kotlin/ktorm.tuples-codegen.gradle.kts` to check the declarations and adjacency relationships of the current kts module, then use the discovery entry point exposed by the current file. Save at least two pieces of trial output: the generated directory's relative path and the status returned by the tool. The path identifies which directory the subsequent compilation receives; the status distinguishes "no directory found" from "directory found but wiring failed." Do not collapse the two into a single boolean.

Observe the Maven lifecycle stage by stage. If the generation stage produces no directory, the issue remains at directory discovery; if the directory has been found but the compile task is not wired up, then inspect the connection from the generation stage to the compilation stage. Do not keep only the final compilation error, as that would obscure the result of directory discovery itself. The broader scope of Maven Lifecycle Applicability still sits alongside DOC-23; this proposal uses it only as a navigation aid and does not promise support for lifecycle combinations that have not been checked.

As of 10/9, KSP-217 had already seen QA reproduction activity. This shows that callers can reproduce the public API track, but it cannot replace an upgrade example covering directory wiring. The open task for KSP-222 is still to follow the discovery entry point in the current file and save the relative path and the status returned by the tool; until both pieces of evidence are available, the upgrade regression must not be marked as passed.

## Trade-offs and Rollback

Having Maven calculate the directory directly keeps the chain short, but makes the extension responsible for more lifecycle differences; having KSP provide directory information gives clearer boundaries but requires handling compatibility with older extensions; a thin adapter is easiest to roll back but may leave duplicate configuration. The plan is to try the second option first, passing only values Maven already knows to the extension and keeping directory discovery results as a separate output.

If the new wiring works in only a single Maven lifecycle phase, or can discover the directory but cannot pass it to the compile task, roll back the directory adapter and keep the existing build conventions. If API regression testing can only prove that internal functions are called and cannot read the caller-visible results of `getCompilerPluginId` or `getPluginOptions`, do not release this public-surface change; go back to the interface examples and redefine the boundary.

Still undecided are the compatibility scope for older Maven projects and what form errors should take when directory discovery fails. Implementation sign-off remains with the technical team; the security review can check versions, environments, and CI failure points, but does not replace the implementation team's decisions on API and lifecycle wiring.

The earlier investigation started at `buildSrc/src/main/kotlin/ktorm.tuples-codegen.gradle.kts`. Declarations related to plugins, builds, source code, and compilation are visible there, but at the time they weren't enough to confirm that Maven's actual compilation phase had run KSP.

2. Record whether the first processing run produces generated sources, along with any diagnostics emitted at the same time.
3. Run processing again without changing the input, and compare the generated sources and diagnostics from the two runs.

If the first run produces results and the second is the same: continue checking the lifecycle wiring and generated source location. If results or diagnostics appear only on the second run: keep a diff of the two sets of generated sources, and don't attribute the cause to KSP yet. If neither run produces results: stop at these two questions: "Did processing actually run?" and "Did the input reach that phase?"

When the example generates output but the Maven entry point produces no results, save the example input, entry-point input, and their respective outputs side by side; don't treat the example's results as proof that the lifecycle is wired up.
